paras: The attempted lynching at Hot Springs, Arkansas, was a failed attempt by armed, masked white men to break into the Hot Springs jail on the night of September 9-10, 1881, and lynch a Black prisoner charged with attempting to outrage an elderly woman, Mrs. J. Parker. The attackers were driven off by gunfire from the jail guards and from Black men who had gathered nearby, and the accounts differed on whether anyone was hurt. A month later, dispatches reported that a Black boy supposed to be the accused, who had escaped, was found dead near Malvern and "must have" been lynched by a pursuing posse. The case drew notice because Black residents armed themselves to defend the prisoner, which a Chicago Tribune dispatch said caused "intense indignation."

According to a Hot Springs dispatch of September 10 printed in the Chicago Tribune, a Black man was charged with attempting to outrage Mrs. J. Parker, "an elderly lady," on September 9. A shorter wire version said a "colored boy" had assaulted Mrs. J. W. Parker, "a lady nearly seventy years of age," and had been arrested and lodged in jail. Other briefs called him only "a negro charged with rape"; no September report named him.

On the night after the arrest, a body of armed men surrounded the jail and tried to break in. The Tribune dispatch said they were met by "a steady fire" from the jail guards and from about a hundred Black men lying in ambush a short distance away, and that more than a hundred shots were fired. A brief carried by Midwestern weeklies instead placed the Black party, which had learned of the plan, in a cemetery and put the shots at about two hundred. The longer wire version said the Black residents "got the news" and hid in the woods, fired about a hundred shots as the masked men approached, and forced the white men, who fired a few shots "at random," to withdraw. That version added that about half of the Black men "broke and ran."

Casualty reports differed: the Tribune dispatch said nobody had yet been found wounded or killed and the cemetery brief said "nobody was killed," while the longer wire version said one white man was wounded.

No report of arrests among the attackers or the Black defenders appears in the coverage. On October 14, specials from Hot Springs relayed through St. Louis reported a Black boy found dead between Hot Springs and Malvern. He was "supposed to be Dick Ellison," who had attempted to outrage Mrs. Jacob Parker and had escaped, and the dispatch concluded that he "must have fallen into the hands of the pursuing posse and been lynched." The report did not say how the accused escaped or how he died, and no confirmation of the identification or report of an inquest was found.

All of the coverage appeared in white newspapers, and it traced to a few wire texts. The Chicago Tribune ran the first dispatch on September 11 under the heading "A Feeling of Indignation," and its page summary spoke of "Intense Indignation" over the defeat of a "Lynching Expedition." That dispatch called the charge "the most heinous of crimes" and reported indignation that "the negroes should attempt to defend" it. The cemetery brief ran in Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan weeklies between September 14 and 24, usually among other crime items.

The longer version, which called the prisoner "the culprit," appeared from September 17 to 24 in papers in Tennessee, Alabama, Arkansas, Missouri, Kansas, Indiana and Louisiana, among them the Huntsville Gazette and the Batesville Guard. In a one-line note, the Kirksville Weekly Graphic called the prisoner a man "guilty of an attempt at rape."

The October report ran from October 14 to 16 in papers in Memphis, Richmond, Savannah, Knoxville, St. Paul, Wheeling and Dallas, under headings such as "A Supposed Lynching" and "Probably Lynched," several giving the woman's name as "Mrs. Jacob Park."

The accounts differ on who fired on the attackers: the Tribune dispatch named the jail guards and the Black men, while the other versions credited only the Black men, and they also disagree on the number of shots and on casualties.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at Hot Springs, Arkansas (1881)
bases: Armed, masked white men tried to break into the Hot Springs jail to lynch a Black prisoner charged with attempted outrage and were driven off by gunfire (A2, A4, A8); a later dispatch supposed the escaped accused was lynched by a posse (A16).

The jail attack by 'a body of armed men' acting on a rape charge killed no one (A2, A4); the only report of a death, a Black boy found dead near Malvern and 'supposed' to be the escaped accused, says only that he 'must have' been lynched by a posse, without confirming identity or cause (A16, A22).

Three distinct wire texts (A2, A4, A8) agree that masked or armed white men went to the jail to lynch the prisoner and were driven off by Black men's gunfire, though they differ on details and casualties; the October death rests on a single dispatch stated as supposition (A16).

accounts.label: Hot Springs special to the Chicago Tribune
accounts.gist: Armed men surrounded the jail the night of Sept. 9 and were met by fire from the jail guards and about a hundred Black men in ambush; over a hundred shots, no one yet known hurt; trouble anticipated.

accounts.label: Cemetery brief (weekly roundups)
accounts.gist: Masked white men went to the jail on the 10th; Black men who learned of the plan gathered in a cemetery and fired; about two hundred shots, nobody killed.

accounts.label: Parker/woods wire version
accounts.gist: A 'colored boy' who assaulted Mrs. J. W. Parker was jailed; next morning masked men came; Black men hidden in the woods fired about a hundred shots; the white men withdrew; half the Black men ran; one white man was wounded.

accounts.label: St. Louis dispatch from Hot Springs specials, Oct. 14
accounts.gist: A Black boy found dead between Hot Springs and Malvern was supposed to be Dick Ellison, the escaped accused, and 'must have' been lynched by the pursuing posse.

framing.detail: The Tribune headed the dispatch 'A Feeling of Indignation', called the charge 'the most heinous of crimes' and reported indignation that Black men defended the prisoner.
Weekly roundups ran the cemetery brief or the Parker version, presenting the prisoner as 'the culprit' and the shooting as a crime-news item.
October follow-ups ran under 'A Supposed Lynching' and 'Probably Lynched', reporting the posse lynching as supposition without comment.
